title: Thermal tolerance, swimming capacity and stress recovery of invasive pink salmon across marine life stages
content:
Abstract
As pink salmon rapidly invade the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans, their physiological performance in newly colonized systems remains largely uncharacterized, limiting our ability to predict their ecological impact on native species. Here, we measured thermal tolerance, swimming capacity and stress recovery in two marine life stages of Atlantic-colonizing pink salmon. Juvenile and mature pink salmon (0.4 and 1.5 kg, respectively) were acclimated to 9°C and 34‰ seawater before completing standardized critical thermal maximum (CTmax) and critical swimming speed (Ucrit) protocols. Blood plasma metrics were measured in unstressed controls, immediately following each stressor and after overnight recovery. Both life stages reached a CTmax of ~26.1°C and a Ucrit range of 113–130 cm s−1. As pink salmon grew, absolute Ucrit increased while relative Ucrit decreased, whereas CTmax tended to decline with size. Both life stages demonstrated robust recovery capacity, with most blood plasma metrics returning towards unstressed levels following overnight recovery. Post-stress mortality was low across both life stages and stressors. Acute warming induced more severe osmoregulatory and acid–base disturbances, while exhaustive exercise elicited a greater cortisol response. Life stage-dependent differences were most apparent in plasma Na+ and glucose, where mature fish showed greater and more prolonged disturbances than juveniles, likely reflecting differences in gill osmoregulation and utilization of energetic reserves. Collectively, these findings provide the first controlled physiological performance and recovery data for pink salmon in their invaded Atlantic range.
